item.title: Images Emerge From Quake-Battered Colombia
item.description:
Shortly after 7:30 on Monday morning, the most powerful earthquake to hit Colombia in a decade sent people fleeing for safety as buildings teetered and then fell.

The epicenter was in a less populous rural area off the Pacific Coast, potentially blunting its effect, but even so, by midafternoon, Colombian officials were reporting that at least 111 people had been confirmed dead.

More than 1,500 residential buildings were damaged, they said, some of them irreparably. At least 20 buildings collapsed in the city of Cali, trapping people inside, according to its mayor.

Eighteen health centers and dozens of schools were also damaged, and air service to more than half a dozen cities was suspended.

Here is a look at some of the first images coming out of Colombia.

Digging through the debris of a collapsed building in Cali.

Covered bodies in a street in Cali.

Damage to the cathedral in Manizales.

A woman after being rescued from a collapsed building in Cali.

Manizales was among the cities hit.

item.title: An Electric Motorcycle Revolution
item.description:
I went to Pakistan last month to write an article about the country’s electric motorcycle boom. I visited showrooms, toured an assembly plant and interviewed company founders and would-be bike buyers. As the trip neared its end, I figured I’d learned just about everything I needed to know.

Except what it feels like to actually ride one.

And then came my moment of fortune. Or maybe misfortune. Depending on how you feel about Lahore’s roads.

“Do you want take it out for a drive?” Abdul Rafay, the owner of a new Vlektra electric motorcycle, asked after we finished an interview.

I looked out at a nearby intersection in this city of 14 million, as motorbikes pinballed around rickshaws and four-wheelers, and muttered something about journalists not making themselves a part of the story.

But OK, I’d accept a ride. So I borrowed a helmet and climbed on the back of Rafay’s bike, just one among the hundreds of thousands of newish, gasoline-free vehicles humming along across Pakistan.

As my article, which came out today, shows, all those motorcycles are emblematic of the big global changes spurred by the war in Iran. By jacking up oil prices, the war has unintentionally accelerated the clean energy transition in developing countries, particularly by influencing the decisions people are making about what kind of vehicle to purchase.

In many of the nations most vulnerable to higher gasoline prices, the most common vehicles tend to have two wheels, not four. And so, in those countries, the electric motorcycle era seems to have arrived.

As I hung on tight, Rafay, 24, took off from the coffee shop where we’d had our interview and merged into a roundabout. We were in a relatively upscale part of the city, with painted lane markers and smooth roads. But drivers in Pakistan, I think it can be said, have a strong stomach for adventure. They are undeterred by streets that can be clogged with traffic or flooded, and often both.

And Rafay clearly wanted to show off his new bike’s power. So he seized on a small opening and accelerated past a rickshaw.

Then, on a long straightaway, he wove past bikes and cars. He zipped toward two orange vehicles, two or three feet apart. Just as Rafay darted between them, the gap opened just enough to let us through.

I was taking a video with my iPhone, and can see in retrospect that the whole maneuver was beautifully orchestrated. But video doesn’t convey my sense of visceral certainty that one of those orange vehicles was going to clip my knee.

I’d clenched my legs hard enough that Rafay could feel it.

“You got scared, didn’t you?” he asked, looking back.

“Yes,” I said, heart racing a bit, but happy.

Hey, who says reporting on climate change has to be grim?

Oh, and the motorcycle: The ride felt smooth. And it surely had enough juice.

Now, I don’t exactly have the résumé to work at Car and Driver. I haven’t driven a motorcycle since 2012, during a vacation misadventure in Vietnam. And even though I live in Italy, the land of the Vespa, I exclusively operate a hatchback with two child car seats.

But that’s why I’d wanted to talk to Rafay. He’s a gearhead who said he’d loved his previous motorcycle, a Honda CD 70, Pakistan’s most popular gas model. He’d driven it 40 miles each day to his job as a software engineer and back home. That is, until gasoline costs soared and he started thinking about the math.

“If I can save a few rupees,” he said, “I’ll do it.”

So after the energy shock driven by the Iran war, Rafay started visiting showrooms of electric motorcycle and scooter brands. He described staying in dealerships sometimes past his welcome, speaking not just with employees but also with other buyers.

He ultimately selected a motorcycle model that he thought could handle all the challenges of Pakistan’s roads. And to be sure, I saw those challenges during my time in Lahore. Some afternoons, monsoon rains would water-bomb the city, inundating lower-lying areas, or any zone with poor drainage, with shin-high water. Life went on during these floods, as did the motorcycle traffic. But it became clear during those moments that motorcycles, whether gas-powered or electric, have big disadvantages. Drivers get soaked.

After my ride with Rafay, I thanked him for driving so capably and handed back the helmet.

Then, before the next rains came, I returned to the Toyota I’d been using for the week. It was a vehicle that never made me clench my knees.

Read the full story.

item.title: Total Eclipse
item.description:
A total solar eclipse is happening today. It’s the first that mainland Europe has seen in nearly 30 years. For a couple of minutes, the moon will line up perfectly with the sun and cast a shadow that plunges part of our planet into total darkness.

I’ve seen only a partial solar eclipse — years ago in London — but even that was an eerie experience: The day suddenly drained away, like an apocalyptic dimming of the light. The world in black and white.

My colleague Katrina Miller has experienced totality before, as a science writer and as a human being. Today she writes about what she describes as not just a spiritual and communal event — but also a “cosmic coincidence.”

By Katrina Miller

Millions of eager spectators flocked to the path of the total solar eclipse that swept across North America in 2024. I was one of them.

It was my first time experiencing totality — those fleeting moments after the moon slides between us and the sun, casting a shadow hundreds of thousands of miles long onto Earth that plunges part of our world into ephemeral darkness.

Totality is as eerie as it is breathtaking. As the moon swallows the sun, the air on Earth cools. Shadows sharpen and the light fades, as if someone turned down the brightness at the wrong part of day. Excitement dissolves into tension as the sun gives one final, brilliant glint. Then the moon clicks into place, and the world is thrown into twilight.

Nature responds to this shift: Birds stop singing, crickets start chirping and flowers close their blooms. Humans react, too. We cheer, gasp and roar below a blotted-out sun, the only time we can stare directly at the star that gives us life.

A cosmic coincidence

Totality is a cosmic coincidence. Our moon is about 400 times smaller than the sun, but it is also 400 times closer to Earth. This makes the two appear to be the same size from our point of view. The sun, moon and Earth are locked in a gravitational dance around one another, and when these three align, we bear witness to a solar eclipse.

Scientists know enough about the movement of bodies in the solar system to predict down to the second when an eclipse will occur. (NASA maintains a list of solar eclipse dates and locations through the end of the century. Read it here.) Today, the event will kick off in northern Russia, and then loop around to Greenland, through Iceland and across the Atlantic Ocean. It will pass over Spain and a tiny corner of Portugal before ending in the Mediterranean Sea.

Those in regions adjacent to the path will see a partial solar eclipse, during which the moon will obscure only a portion of the sun’s surface. But people along the eclipse path itself — a swath of land less than 322 kilometers wide, delineated by the shadow of the moon — will, weather permitting, get about two minutes of totality.

Humans, on a rock, in space

Before the main event in 2024, I spent months learning about the history and science of solar eclipses, how to stay safe viewing one and the effects they have on living things. But nothing could have prepared me for what many eclipse chasers describe as a spiritual experience.

Facts and figures don’t quell the unease of watching the light die, nor do they dampen the relief felt when it reappears on the other side. Skywatchers along the eclipse path breathe a collective sigh as they emerge from the moon’s shadow, almost like a wave that ripples through the crowd at a sporting event, but on a global scale.

There’s a certain kinship fostered under a total solar eclipse. People spend months, even years, preparing for an event that lasts but a few moments. In the hours leading up to totality, we congregate in stadiums, on the sides of highways, atop pyramids and on boats in the sea. We don our eclipse glasses, and, together, we turn our gaze to the sky.

Totality is a heady reminder that we are on a rock twirling around a star in space, part of a system of planets within a galaxy that exists inside of an infinite universe. But more than that, it offers a primal sense of what it means to be human, through shared despair and delight under a celestial rebirth. We are all so consumed by our problems on the ground. Sometimes, we need a reason to look up.

Looking at the sun with the unaided eye, even for a few seconds, can cause permanent damage.

item.title: What We Know About the Earthquake in Colombia
item.description:
A major earthquake struck Colombia on Monday, killing more than 100 people, damaging hundreds of buildings in the country’s west and prompting a frantic search for survivors.

The 7.4-magnitude earthquake was the most powerful recorded in the South American nation in the past decade, the Colombian Geological Survey said.

President Abelardo De La Espriella of Colombia, who had been sworn into office just three days before the quake, declared a state of emergency and said that he would directly lead the disaster response.

Here’s what to know.

The epicenter of the quake, according to the U.S. Geological Survey, was about three miles east of San José del Palmar — a town of about 5,000 people in the Chocó region, one of the poorest parts of Colombia.

The temblor, which struck about 7:34 a.m. local time, rattled much of the country, though the impact was worst in cities and towns in the foothills of the Andes.

Major damage was reported in Cali, the country’s third-largest city, which has about two million residents. The cities of Pereira and Manizales, hubs of Colombia’s coffee-growing region that are each home to about 500,000 people, were also badly hit.

The country’s two largest cities — Bogotá, the capital, and Medellín — appeared to have escaped the worst of the damage. But residents there and across the country reported intense shaking.

The quake was also felt in neighboring countries including Panama, Ecuador and Venezuela, though there were no reports of serious damage.

The earthquake killed at least 111 people and injured 87 others, according to Mr. De La Espriella. The death toll was expected to rise as rescuers and residents dug through rubble.

Rescue efforts were underway across western Colombia. In Cali, Mayor Alejando Eder said that emergency workers were focusing on finding people in debris from 10 collapsed buildings. Mayor Carlos Fernando Galán of Bogotá said the city was preparing to send rescue crews to hard-hit cities.

It is unclear how long people can survive trapped in rubble after an earthquake, researchers say. But some experts say that there is a 72-hour “golden” window in which the most lives can be saved.

The quake damaged at least 1,575 homes, 18 health centers and 52 schools, Mr. De La Espriella said.

In Cali, at least 26 buildings collapsed, trapping people inside, according to its mayor. In Calima El Darién, a town north of Cali, a hospital collapsed and another was overwhelmed with victims.

There was also widespread damage, including piles of rubble from collapsed buildings, in Pereira and Manziales. Several airports in western Colombia, including in Pereira and Manziales, were among the structures damaged, according to the Colombian Civil Aviation Authority.

The agency said it had suspended operations at some airports until structural damage could be assessed.

The earthquake is the first big test for Mr. De La Espriella, a right-wing former lawyer with no previous political experience who was sworn in on Friday after winning the presidential election in June.

He said in a video posted on social media on Monday that he had canceled his travel plans to head to Bogotá, where he said he would “personally assume leadership” of the emergency response.

“You’re not alone,” he wrote, addressing people affected by the disaster. “The state is present and taking action.”

item.title: Russia Releases Former U.S. Marine After 4 Years in Prison
item.description:
Russia released an American who had been held in prison for more than four years, and he was en route to the United States on Tuesday, President Trump said.

The release of the detainee, Robert Gilman, 32, a Massachusetts resident and former Marine, came after his family and an advocacy group sounded the alarm about his failing health and accused Russia of mistreating him.

Mr. Trump wrote on social media on Tuesday, “I am proud to announce that American Citizen Robert Gilman, a former United States Marine, is coming HOME!” He added that after discussions with President Vladimir V. Putin, “Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis,” and “asked for no one in return.”

Mr. Gilman had been imprisoned in Voronezh, Russia, since early in 2022, when a court convicted him of assaulting a police officer and ultimately sentenced him to 10 years in prison. His health had significantly deteriorated since then, according to his family and a statement from Global Reach, a nonprofit organization representing Mr. Gilman and other Americans wrongly held abroad.

He was in a dire state when he was recently transferred to a Russian civilian hospital, prompting his family and the State Department to call for his release on humanitarian grounds.

For many weeks, according to Global Reach, Mr. Gilman had been in a “dissociative stupor,” in which a patient is unresponsive without an apparent physical cause. When he lands back in the United States, he will be taken to a military hospital in Texas, where he will be medically and psychologically assessed, his advocates said, and he will reunite with his family.

“It is too early to know Robert’s long-term medical prognosis,” said Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer of the advocacy group.

Mr. Gilman’s family and Global Reach have accused the Russian authorities of detaining him for political purposes and severely abusing him.

In a Global Reach statement on Tuesday, Lexie Hudson, Mr. Gilman’s sister, accused Russia of hurting him “for no reason, other than that he was both and American and a Marine.” She expressed gratitude to Mr. Trump for her brother’s release, crediting him with saving his life.

Mr. Gilman’s parents originally moved from Russia to Dracut, Mass., his father, Vladimir Gilman, wrote in a 2024 Boston Globe article. Robert Gilman was born in Poland and raised in Massachusetts, later serving in the Marines. He traveled to Moldova in early 2022 to explore a teaching opportunity but fell ill while transiting through Russia and decided to recuperate there, his father wrote.

While on a train, Mr. Gilman fell ill and was taken to a local police station, where, his father wrote, he accidentally kicked a police officer. He was initially sentenced to four and a half years in a penal colony.

“This event would normally result in a fine or a suspended sentence, if anything,” his father wrote in 2024. “But Robert was singled out because he is an American.”

Last year, the sentence was extended to a decade in prison, after the authorities said Mr. Gilman had assaulted prison staff and an investigator, according to Russian news agencies.

Mr. Trump’s statement on Tuesday suggested that the former Marine’s health may have improved. He said that Mr. Gilman would first land at Andrews Air Force Base in Washington.

“I just spoke to him, and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands,” Mr. Trump said. “I will take care of that!”

The State Department on Tuesday thanked Russia for working with Steve Witkoff, Mr. Trump’s special envoy, on Mr. Gilman’s release. “While we appreciate this positive step, we are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans, including wrongful detainee Stephen Hubbard,” it said in a statement.

Mr. Hubbard, a retired American teacher, was taken from his home in eastern Ukraine by Russian soldiers shortly after Russia invaded in February 2022. He was located in a Russian prison last year. Mr. Hubbard, who is in his 70s, was accused by Russia of working at military checkpoints and fighting for Ukraine. He was convicted of being a mercenary and sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony.

Global Reach, in its statement on Tuesday, noted that there were five additional Americans being held in Russia, saying “it is critical that the administration uses the momentum of Robert’s release” to bring them home.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted the State Department statement about Mr. Gillman’s release on social media, along with an image showing the former Marine on his flight. Wearing a cap, he looked emaciated, pale and haggard, but was smiling and surrounded by a people in the airplane’s aisle holding an American flag.

“The President will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home,” Mr. Rubio said.

Isabella Kwai contributed reporting.

item.title: Six Killed in Houthi Strikes on Red Sea Ship, Yemeni Government Says
item.description:
At least six people were killed on Tuesday when a cargo ship was hit in the Red Sea by missiles fired by the Houthi militia, Yemen’s government said, an escalation in the chaos that has engulfed shipping in the Middle East.

The Yemeni Transport Ministry said in a statement that the vessel Tihamah was carrying food supplies and was hit while transiting the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. The ministry added that four crew members — three Pakistanis and one Indonesian — were killed when a fire broke out on board.

Later on Tuesday, the Yemeni Coast Guard said that two members of Yemen’s armed forces were also killed during a rescue mission, when another Houthi missile targeted the vessel.

The Houthi military released a short statement confirming that its forces targeted a ship in the Bab al-Mandab Strait and alleged that the vessel was carrying “Saudi military equipment.” The group has in recent weeks fired on Saudi-linked oil vessels in the Red Sea and said it was imposing a maritime blockade against the kingdom, after deadly clashes with the Saudi-backed government in Yemen.

The deaths on Tuesday mark the first-known fatalities in the Red Sea from Houthi fire since the start of the broader U.S.-Israeli war with Iran in February.

There was no immediate comment from the Saudi, Pakistani and Indonesian governments.

There are conflicting accounts of the ship’s ownership. While the Transport Ministry described the Tihamah as a “Yemeni commercial vessel,” the shipping database Equasis says that it is a small cargo ship owned by an Egyptian company, Thubab for Marine Services, and flies the Tanzanian maritime flag.

The Yemeni government accused the Houthis, an Iran-backed militia based in northern Yemen, of expanding their targets in the Red Sea. “This poses a direct threat to food supplies and consumer goods for millions of Yemenis,” the Transport Ministry said.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, which is administered by Britain’s Royal Navy, said Tuesday that a vessel was struck by an unidentified projectile off the Yemeni port of Mokha and that casualties were reported.

The attack threatens to further imperil a crucial maritime transit route. The Red Sea has grown in importance since Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for oil and gas shipping in the Persian Gulf, at the start of the war.

Saudi Arabia, in particular, has relied on the Red Sea as an alternative export route for its oil, but, last month, the Houthis announced a maritime embargo against the kingdom and have fired on its vessels.

Even so, traffic through the Bab al-Mandab Strait has remained steady. Kpler, a maritime analytics firm, logged 36 vessel crossings on Monday, up one from the day before.

The deadly attack in the Red Sea coincides with a spike in violence in Yemen itself, as the Houthis have carried out missile and drone strikes on government-controlled cities. The Yemeni government has launched counterattacks on rebel forces, and the escalating violence threatens to tip the country back into full-scale civil war.

The two sides have been locked in conflict since 2014, when the Houthis seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, with Iranian support. A Saudi-led military coalition intervened the following year to restore the government to power, but a devastating bombing campaign ultimately failed to oust the Houthi rebels.

A United Nations-brokered cease-fire was agreed on in 2022, and the conflict has since been stalemated, leaving Yemen essentially divided in two, with the Houthis controlling the north. Observers now say the truce is close to a breaking point.

In statements posted late Monday, Mohammed Abdulsalam, the Houthis’ chief negotiator, framed the group’s escalating operations in recent weeks as a “legitimate response” to foreign military action. Mr. Abdulsalam accused Saudi Arabia of waging economic war on Yemen during the four-year truce by stopping ships heading to the Houthi-controlled port city of Hodeidah and imposing sanctions on local banks.

Peter Eavis contributed reporting.

item.title: Shouting Names, Hoping for Replies and Digging for Survivors of Colombian Quake
item.description:
The crowd chanted her name: “Diana! Diana!”

As search and rescue efforts continued the day after a deadly earthquake in Colombia, firefighters toiled in searing heat on Tuesday to pull a 31-year-old biomedical engineer from the rubble of a collapsed building in the city of Cali.

Diana Marcela Troncoso had been trapped for almost 30 hours. She was limp, save for a hand that gripped the arm of a firefighter like a lifeline. She cried in pain as they strapped her to a backboard. But she was alive.

Desperate searches for survivors of Colombia’s strongest earthquake in a decade continued on Tuesday throughout the western part of the country.

The death toll from the 7.4-magnitude quake had risen to at least 181 people, according to Asocapitales, an association of Colombian cities, with at least 1,310 people injured and 153 buildings collapsed. Because communication is still down in some affected areas, officials said they expected the numbers to rise.

The highest toll appeared to be in Cali, the country’s third-largest city, which is known as a hub of culture, music and dance. The city, about 100 miles south of the epicenter, was supposed to spend the week celebrating an annual music festival known as Petronio, a cherished tradition that attracts thousands of revelers.

Instead, the quake hit Monday morning, causing at least 45 structures to collapse. As of Tuesday, more than 230 people were trapped alive in the rubble, according to local officials. And firefighters and aid groups have come streaming in from Bogotá, the capital, and beyond.

It was Bogotá firefighters who helped pull Ms. Troncoso from the rubble. People clapped and cheered them on as they carried her down a mountain of crumbled concrete.

“She works to save lives,” said her cousin, Andrés Troncoso, once she had been placed in a waiting ambulance. “And fortunately today it was her turn, and she was saved.”

The U.S. State Department said Tuesday that it was sending a disaster response team to support rescue operations, on top of committing $15.5 million in aid for emergency shelter, food, protection and earthquake assessments.

The United Nations and other international aid groups have also pledged support.

The scenes at collapsed buildings in Cali contrasted sharply with those that had played out just a few weeks earlier in Venezuela, where back-to-back powerful quakes killed at least 6,300 people.

Venezuela’s disaster was far larger and harder to tackle, and in the wake of that disaster, it was civilians who carried out much of the search and rescue effort, with the state often absent. Emergency teams had been crippled by years of budget cuts under an authoritarian government focused on its own survival, and the teams that remained in operation lacked the tools to carry out complex rescue missions.

Rescue attempts were often chaotic as everyday people debated what to do, with no clear chain of command. Many Venezuelans said that they felt abandoned by the government in their time of need.

But in Cali, at several collapsed buildings on Monday and Tuesday, it was state emergency workers running operations, sometimes cordoning off the area with yellow tape while civilians helped remove rubble on the sidelines. At one building on Monday night, an ambulance stood at the ready. A yellow construction machine was used to haul away some heavy concrete.

Yet in both countries, the emergencies are testing new leaders, both of whom have the strong support of President Trump.

In Venezuela, the disaster response has hardened popular anger at President Delcy Rodríguez, who took power in January following the U.S. capture of her predecessor.

Colombia’s new president, Abelardo De La Espriella, a lawyer who had never held office, took office just three days before the quakes hit, promising to focus on places beyond the capital.

He visited the western city of Pereira on Tuesday, meeting with officials and assessing damaged buildings. He has said repeatedly since the quake that victims will not be abandoned.

On Tuesday, representatives of several foreign governments said they were waiting on a green light from the De La Espriella government to send aid, including expert rescuers.

“We hope the Colombian government immediately announces the name of the official and their official liaison for coordinating international assistance,” the Chinese ambassador to Colombia wrote on X. “Please help us share this message — it is urgent!”

Nayib Bukele, the president of El Salvador wrote on X that Colombia had requested supplies, but no rescue teams. “We have been informed that their rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency units are already deployed and managing the situation,” he said.

Mexico’s leaders said they had readied an aid team and were waiting for permission from Colombia to deploy.

And a representative for the U.N. said at a news briefing that Mr. De La Espriella’s government had not made an official request for international aid, adding that the U.N. was standing by to provide all the help it could.

A member of Mr. De La Espriella’s press team did not respond to a request for comment.

Beyond Cali, cities in Colombia’s coffee-growing region, including Pereira and Manizales on the western flank of the Andes, were heavily affected by the quake, as was the Chocó region on the Pacific Coast.

The governor of Chocó, one of the poorest areas of Colombia, said Tuesday on national radio that the full extent of the devastation was not yet known, in part because communications were still down in eight municipalities in her department.

“What we don’t have is a complete tally of the physical damage,” said the governor, Nubia Carolina Córdoba Curi, “because it is truly massive.”

In Cali, rescue efforts were sure to continue long into the night, with firefighters desperately trying to find people in the critical first 48 hours after the disaster.

At one collapsed residential building in the Tequendama neighborhood on Monday evening, firefighters, paramedics and other rescuers clawed through the debris to try to find a family of four they believed was trapped inside, while civilians formed human chains to haul away buckets of dust and rubble.

“We believe they’re there because we heard them screaming,” said Daniel Leguizamo, a 16-year-old paramedic with a private rescue squad who rushed to Cali from the city of Popayán shortly after the quake.

Katerín Carrillo, 32, a local business owner, said she and friends handed out water, electrolyte drinks and homemade sandwiches, taking them to rescue sites after learning about the damage online.

“We washed our hands with alcohol and made sandwiches right in the vehicle,” Ms. Carrillo said. “The people who are hauling rocks over there should at least have something to eat.”

Amid the debris lay remnants of lives disrupted: a scrapbook called “my 15 years” filled with old photographs, a “my first year” poster, a shoe, a piece of zebra wallpaper. Collected items pulled from the building were placed in bins, which people searched to recover what they could.

When rescuers needed quiet, people raised their hands and the signal rippled through the crowd.
